title: The great commandment
hook: love God, love your neighbor: all of it in two lines
tomorrow: how can anyone call people who mourn "blessed"?

segments.voice: Yesterday, amen once more: the crowd's answer, God's yes, and a name. Let it be so. Now a new week, and the last stretch up the hill.

It's the kind of question that goes around a comment thread: if you could keep just one rule, which one? In Matthew it's asked out loud, as a test, with people watching for a slip. An expert in the law puts it to Jesus: "Master, which is the great commandment in the law?" There are plenty to choose from. Everyone leans in to hear which one he'll pick.
screen: `JUST ONE RULE?` → `A TEST, IN PUBLIC.` → `WHICH IS THE GREAT COMMANDMENT?`

segments.voice: He doesn't pick one. He picks two, and both come out of scripture his listeners already knew. "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The first comes from Deuteronomy, right after the words Hear, O Israel, which Deuteronomy says to talk of when you lie down and when you rise up. Jews still pray those words, the Shema: shared ground at the very root of this answer. The second comes from Leviticus, from a chapter of everyday rules about leaving some harvest for the poor, paying wages on time, and never tripping up the blind. One to tell a friend tonight: "love thy neighbour as thyself" was scripture before Jesus quoted it. He sets the two side by side and says the second is like the first. Love for God and love for the person next to you aren't two projects. They're one love, facing two ways. Then the line that names this day: "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." Hang, like a door on two hinges. Take either one away and the door falls. Churches work out the details differently. The hinges stay the same.
screen: `NOT ONE: TWO.` · `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `LEVITICUS: YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `TWO HINGES, ONE DOOR.` · then, large: `ON THESE TWO.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and hold two faces in mind. First, turn toward God with one honest line of love or thanks, or toward whatever you hold most dear. Then turn toward one neighbor you'll see soon, and wish them, by name, the good you'd want for yourself.
The great commandment. Love God with all you are, and your neighbor as yourself: two lines from the Hebrew Scriptures, with everything hanging on them.
Keep this: on these two, two hinges and one door that swings on both. Day done.

howItsDone: Some churches read Jesus's summary of the law aloud near the start of worship, and Christians learn the two commandments in Sunday school and catechism as a summary of how to live.

chat.meaning: Asked for the great commandment, Jesus gives two, from Deuteronomy and Leviticus, and says all the law and the prophets hang on them.

Deuteronomy.meaning: the fifth book of the Bible, Moses's last teaching

Leviticus.meaning: a book of the law about worship and everyday holiness

Shema.meaning: Hear, O Israel: words from Deuteronomy that Jews pray

the law and the prophets.meaning: a way of naming the Hebrew Scriptures

sources.quoted: Master, which is the great commandment in the law?

Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: story: the public test question as a scene, answered in the teach). Title, word, carry and sources kept; Matthew 22:36 now quoted.
Matthew 22:35 calls the questioner 'a lawyer' who asked 'tempting him'; the script says 'an expert in the law' and 'a test' and leaves his group unnamed so no one is the foil.
'Jews still pray those words, the Shema: shared ground' refers to Deuteronomy 6:4–9, offered as a neighbor's practice with no comparison. Please confirm the phrasing with a Keeper.
Leviticus 19 details: gleanings left for the poor (19:9–10), wages paid on time (19:13), no stumbling block before the blind (19:14), love thy neighbour (19:18).
'Love thy neighbour as thyself was scripture before Jesus quoted it' rests on Leviticus 19:18, cited.
'Hang, like a door on two hinges' is an image, not a claim about the Greek verb.
